7.0.s.en: 1. The alliance of Rezin and Pekah against Ahaz:

7.0.0.en: 1 And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.

7.0.1.en: At the beginning of Ahaz's reign, Rezin king of Syria allied himself with Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, against Judah [1]. The first attacked from the direction of Transjordan, while the second rushed in with his armies from the north, and Ahaz was defeated. They went up to Jerusalem, the capital, to besiege it, but they were not able to storm it. The cause of the battle was the political disagreement between Ahaz and the other two kings; Ahaz saw fit to ally himself with Assyria, while the two kings saw fit to ally themselves with Egypt.

7.0.2.en: Ahaz found himself in a predicament, so he asked for the help of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, who hastened toward Damascus, where he killed Rezin (2 Kgs 16:9), and he did the same also to Samaria (2 Kgs 15:29).

7.1.0.en: 2 And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.

7.1.1.en: When Ahaz learned that Syria had settled in Ephraim (the northern kingdom, or Israel) in order to ally with it against him, “his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind” [2]. Ahaz and his people realized that they were unable to face Syria and Israel, but the true cause of their fear was their lack of faith in God as a support for them, able to fortify them and grant them victory. They lost their inner peace by isolating themselves from God, the source of victory and peace.

7.2.0.en: 3 Then said the LORD unto Isaiah, “Go forth to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field; 4 And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah. 5 Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying, 6 Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal: 7 Thus saith the Lord GOD, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass. 8 For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people. 9 And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah's son. If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”

7.2.1.en: Ahaz was greatly troubled, because he had left out of his calculations the element of faith, or “the divine presence.” He did not call for repentance and a return to God, nor did he go to the temple to lay the matter before God, nor did he send to the prophet to consult him. Rather, he used human means, resorting to Assyria for his protection, and going out to the end of the conduit of the upper pool [3], west of Jerusalem at the head of the valley of the son of Hinnom, to examine with the men of state the sources of water, in order to divert them to the city so that it might benefit from them during the expected siege, and to deprive the enemy of them (2 Chr 22:3-4; Isa 22:9-11), as he was also busy fortifying the city as far as he could.

7.3.0.en: With all this, God intervened, not for the sake of Ahaz, but for the sake of the very few holy ones of His people, and for the sake of David His servant and the city dear to Him. He asked Isaiah to go out to meet Ahaz, together with Shear-jashub (= the remnant shall return), as a sign and a wonder in Israel (Isa 8:8), assuring him: “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah” [4].

7.3.1.en: The prophet and his son met the king at the pool so that God might declare to the king that salvation would not be accomplished by human planning and temporal means, but by the transcendent work of God and His care for His children. The prophet met the king at the pool to assure him that God wants to speak with mankind wherever they are: He meets Levi at the place of tax collection, Zacchaeus at the sycamore tree, the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, and so on... He seeks us and goes to us wherever we are, longing for our salvation more than we ourselves long for it.

7.3.2.en: God asked Ahaz not to fear and not to let his heart grow faint, for these reasons:

7.3.3.en: a. That the two enemies, “Pekah and Rezin,” are nothing but two smoking firebrands [4]. In this way the children of God find resistance and alliances of enemies against them, but all this is no more than a smoking firebrand that clouds the air and offends the nose for a while, without a blazing fire to burn. The enemy of good is strong and mighty in appearance, but he becomes very small and utterly weak before us if we hide in Christ, the Conqueror of the devil and of all his powers.

7.3.4.en: St. John Chrysostom says to Theodore the Fallen:

7.3.5.en: [If Satan has this power to cast you down to the ground from a lofty height and exalted virtue, to the farthest limits of evil, how much more is God able to raise you up to your former confidence, and to make you not only as you were, but happier than before.]

7.4.0.en: b. The failure of the enemies' plot: The two kings made a hidden, satanic plot, but God, who knows all hidden things, declared it so that King Ahaz might take precautions, despite his wickedness and his foolishness. The Lord says, “It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass” [7]. The enemy may succeed at first, reckoning that he is achieving his evil aims, but the Lord scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts (Lk 1:51).

7.5.0.en: c. Syria will not be able to expand as it thought, but will keep to its borders: “For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin” [8]. So however much Rezin may fight, he will return to Damascus, and his kingdom will not expand at the expense of Judah as he supposes. As for Ephraim, within a period of 65 years it will be broken, that it be not reckoned a people [8]; some see that this refers to a period of 5-6 years, that is 11 years, since the captivity of Israel was accomplished 11 years after the word of the prophet Isaiah (2 Kgs 17:3, 6). Yet some scholars see that the prophet is referring here to the ruin of Israel by Esarhaddon, who brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the children of Israel, to put an end to the nation of Israel completely (2 Kgs 17:24).

7.6.0.en: The prophet concluded his speech by saying, “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established” [9]. For unless they believe the divine promise and trust in it, relying on the arm of the Lord, they will not stand firm in these harsh and difficult circumstances. Faith is the shield (1 Thess 5:8) that protects us from the blows of the enemy.

7.6.1.en: This statement appears in the Septuagint as: “If ye will not believe, neither shall ye understand.” St. Augustine commented on it at length; among his words are these:

7.6.2.en: [You cannot obtain understanding unless faith dawns in the heart, which says with the prophet: “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not understand.”]

7.6.3.en: [Faith is sought, but understanding is found, for the prophet says: “Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand.”]

7.6.4.en: [According to the teaching of the Catholic Church, it is fitting for the mind to be nourished first by simple faith, so that it may be able to understand the heavenly, eternal things.]

7.6.5.en: [You (he is addressing the heretics) have not been taught in the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the true, catholic Church of Christ; otherwise you would have drawn from the treasury of the Holy Scriptures what is old and also what is new. The Lord Himself says: “Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” (Mt 13:52).]

7.6.6.en: St. Augustine sees that through faith the Lord Christ accompanies a person, walking with him all the way, as He did with the two disciples of Emmaus who besought Him to stay with them, and when He sat at meat with them, “their eyes were opened, and they knew him” (Lk 24:31).

7.6.7.en: St. Clement of Alexandria comments on the same statement, saying: “This means that if you do not believe what the Law prophesied and receive the teaching of the Law, you will not understand the Old Testament, which He (the Lord Christ) interpreted by His coming.”

7.7.s.en: 4. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign:

7.7.0.en: 10 Moreover the LORD spake again unto Ahaz, saying, 11 “Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” 12 But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD.” 13 And he said, “Hear ye, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?”

7.8.0.en: God offered Ahaz every possibility of salvation, but his heart had become utterly hardened, and he trusted in Assyria and not in God. Even so, God in His love and kindness returned to speak with him through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above” [11]. It is as though He were saying to him: Why do you seek help from Assyria, a stranger? I am your God, ready to confirm my promises to you with a sign from the earth or from heaven, for I am the God of heaven and earth. Ask what you wish and I will give it to you. Ask that an earthquake or a splitting of the earth occur, as happened with Korah and his company, or ask for lightnings or thunders or rains or a sign in the sun, as happened with Joshua when the sun stood still. For although I do not like to give signs for show, yet out of my love for the house of David, and so that you may believe in me, I will give you the desire of your heart. But Ahaz had set his gaze on Assyria, rejecting any help from God, and so he refused to ask for a sign from Him, justifying that with a Scripture text, “neither will I tempt the LORD” [12] (Deut 6:16). He did not say this out of trust in God, but out of a desire not to deal with Him.

7.8.1.en: This passage is read at the Morning Hour on the Friday of the second week of the Great Fast, when the readings focus on “the temptation of the Lord Christ.” It is as though the Spirit of the Lord is affirming that in every age there are wicked people who wish to cover their wickedness with Scripture texts; even Satan himself used the same approach in his dialogue with the Lord Christ at the temptation. How dangerous is the misuse of the word of God!

7.9.0.en: Ahaz was deceitful in his answer even to the Lord, so the prophet rebuked him, saying: “Hear ye, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?” [13]. The people were wearied by the injustices of Ahaz and his household, and now they are like those who weary God by their lack of faith in Him, relying on Assyria and not on the Lord.

7.10.0.en: 14 But the Lord himself shall give you a sign; “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. 15 Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. 16 For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.”

7.10.1.en: Ahaz refused to ask God for a sign that he might be assured that He would save him from Syria and Israel, and behold, the Lord presents Himself as a sign, not to Ahaz alone but to all mankind, that we may be assured that He saves it, not from human arms but from all the powers of wicked darkness, lifting it above temporal events and carrying it with Him into the Father's embrace. At the same time He assures Ahaz that the house of David will not fall completely, but that the Son of David, “the wondrous sign,” will come, who is able to raise up the fallen tabernacle of David.

7.10.2.en: The sign that the Lord wants to give every believer is that He gives Himself, “Immanuel.” We do not deepen the request or raise it on high; rather, like Ahaz, we are afraid to ask, although He waits to give us Himself; He comes down to us to raise us to Himself, so that He may be our good portion that will not be taken from us. For this reason St. Irenaeus says: [What Isaiah said, “Lift up on high and deepen below,” means to point to the One who descended and ascended (Eph 4:10).] Let us ask for this wondrous sign, Immanuel, who came down to us to lift us up to His heavens.

7.10.3.en: Truly it is a unique sign, and as St. John Chrysostom says: [Since what was about to happen was strange, such that many could not believe it even when it was accomplished, He sent first, before everything, prophets to proclaim this truth.]

7.10.4.en: And with the same meaning the martyr Justin says: [The things that seemed unreasonable, and even impossible, to men, God proclaimed by the spirit of prophecy...]

7.10.5.en: a. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” [14]. As the martyr Justin says in his Dialogue with Trypho (66): [It is clear to all that no one in the race of Abraham was born of a virgin, or was said to be, except our Christ.]

7.10.6.en: The virginity of St. Mary is a Gospel truth that hides our faith in Christ Jesus her Son. For the Word of God, at His incarnation, did not care about the kind of place in which He would lie, or the clothes with which He would be swaddled, or the food on which He would feed, but He specified precisely the “virgin” who would become His mother.

7.10.7.en: The Hebrew word used for virgin is “Alma,” and not “virginity,” nor “Isha.” For “Alma” means a young virgin who may be betrothed, whereas “virginity” means an unbetrothed virgin, while Isha means a married woman. It is as though the word “Alma” corresponds exactly to the state of St. Mary, being a virgin and at the same time betrothed to St. Joseph, who was for her a defender and faithful witness to her chastity, whose presence removes every doubt or suspicion about her.

7.10.8.en: The prophet Ezekiel spoke (Ezek 44:1-2) about the virginity of St. Mary:

7.10.9.en: * Ezekiel testified and showed us this, saying:

7.10.10.en: I saw a gate toward the east, the Lord the Savior entered it, and it remained well closed as it was.

7.10.11.en: The Sunday Absalia Adam: the virginity of St. Mary is a proof of our faith in the Lord Christ, that He is not of the seed of man, that He is not of this world, but is the incarnate Son of God, who came to us from on high. She bore “Immanuel,” which means “God with us”; He came down to us incarnate in the virgin womb, to take on our nature and become one with us, dwelling in our midst, sanctifying all that is ours.

7.10.12.en: * Those who proclaimed that He is Immanuel, born of the Virgin (Isa 7:14), proclaimed also the union of the Word of God with the work of His hands.

7.10.13.en: When the Word became flesh, and the Son of God became the son of man, the Pure One opened with purity and the pure womb, giving mankind renewal in God.

7.10.14.en: St. Irenaeus * The Lord Christ opened the womb of the holy Church, that silent womb, without blemish, full of fruit, where the people of God are born.

7.10.15.en: St. Ambrose * Your divine birth, O Lord, has given all mankind a birth... Humanity bore You according to the flesh, and You bore it according to the Spirit... Glory to You, who became a child that You might make all things new.

7.10.16.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * We affirm that the only-begotten Son became man... so that, being born of a woman according to the flesh, He might renew the human race in Himself.

7.11.0.en: St. Cyril the Great b. “Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good” [15].

7.11.1.en: Here the prophet affirms the humanity of the Lord Christ; for though He is not of the seed of man, He truly became the Son of Man, sharing with us our food and our conduct and resembling us in everything except sin alone (Heb 2:7).

7.11.2.en: Butter and honey are the food of little boys, for He did not reach manhood all at once, but passed through the stage of boyhood, during which He knows to refuse evil and choose the good, a sign of the maturity of His soul and mind. We see Him at twelve years of age sitting in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them, until they were astonished at His teaching (Lk 2:46-47).

7.12.0.en: This was fulfilled with regard to our Lord Jesus Christ, born alone of the Virgin; but with regard to what took place in the days of Ahaz, God announced the birth of a son to Isaiah, of whom it was said: “For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings” [16]. This was fulfilled with all precision, for the king of Assyria attacked Damascus a short time after this prophecy was announced and Rezin was killed (2 Kgs 16:9), and Hoshea the son of Elah killed Pekah the son of Remaliah and reigned in his place (2 Kgs 15:30), and 200,000 captives were quickly returned (Shear-jashub = the remnant shall return), and that not by might nor by power but by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Kgs 18:8-15).

7.13.s.en: 6. Assyria, the ally, becomes an enemy:

7.13.0.en: 17 “The LORD shall bring upon thee, and upon thy people, and upon thy father's house, days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah; even the king of Assyria. 18 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. 19 And they shall come, and shall rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes. 20 In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, that a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep; 22 And it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk that they shall give he shall eat butter: for butter and honey shall every one eat that is left in the land. 23 And it shall come to pass in that day, that every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings, it shall even be for briers and thorns. 24 With arrows and with bows shall men come thither; because all the land shall become briers and thorns. 25 And on all hills that shall be digged with the mattock, there shall not come thither the fear of briers and thorns: but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen, and for the treading of lesser cattle.”

7.13.1.en: Since Ahaz leaned on Assyria as his ally without returning to the Lord, God allows Assyria to turn into an enemy against Judah, and Judah passes through a bitterness it had not passed through since the kingdom was divided into two kingdoms, “Israel and Judah” [17]. At the same time it sees difficult days from the side of Egypt, so that Judah becomes like something between two millstones, not in the sense that Assyria and Egypt agree against it, but that the two struggle against each other and Judah becomes the scapegoat for both, with the battles and conflicts taking place in its land.

7.14.0.en: “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly (the armies of Egypt) that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee (the armies of Assyria) that is in the land of Assyria. And they shall come, and shall rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes (that is, the armies will cover all the regions of Judah)” [18-19].

7.15.0.en: The Lord goes on to depict the destruction that Assyria will bring about with a hired razor that shaves the hair of the head, the hair of the feet, and the beard [20]. It is as though the enemy stretches out his hand, as with a razor, to wipe away everything that belongs to the king and his household and the great ones (the head), and what belongs to the common people (the feet), and also the priests (the beard). Thus Assyria turns into a destroying and shattering razor! Shaving the beard was a sign of humiliation, since captives were compelled to submit to it involuntarily.

7.16.0.en: Once again He gives a picture of the destruction of Judah, which was famous for raising sheep, so that every man owned many head; but after the destruction, a man of means has a young cow and two sheep [21], and the good vineyards turn into land of briers and thorns [23], since there are no working hands because of the war...
